newsitem.title: USA: Agouron Viracept outlook remains strong.
newsitem.headline: Agouron Viracept outlook remains strong.

text.p: Agouron Pharmaceuticals' stunning debut in the AIDS drug market will be followed by more strong growth as patients make Viracept their drug of choice, industry analysts and company officials said Friday.

The La Jolla, Calif.-based company Thursday reported sales of its Viracept AIDS drug reached $43.6 million in the fourth quarter, its first full quarter on the market. The number exceeded virtually all forecasts.
Agouron now projects sales in fiscal 1998, which will end June 30, could reach $250 million.

"We've been surprised by the level of demand from the first day we launched the drug," Agouron President and Chief Executive Officer Peter Johnson said Friday. "The only real answer I have is that the attributes of the drug are being appreciated and fairly rapidly accepted by physicians and patients."

One reason the success of Viracept has surprised so many is that the drug is not unique. It belongs to a class known as protease inhibitors, which are also made by other drug companies, including Abbott Laboratories Inc, Merck and Co Inc and Roche Holding Ltd.

Protease inhibitors first came on the market a year ago, and were quickly shown to be one of the most effective ways to control the AIDS virus, when used in combination with two other drugs in a combination known as the "AIDS cocktail."
Agouron's Johnson said that between 80 and 90 percent of the patients who use Viracept as part of a three-drug cocktail see their viral load drop to non-detectable levels.

Although that is an impressive success rate, similar results are reported by the makers of competing drugs, including Merck, whose Crixivan drug is currently the leading protease inhibitor on the market.
But as a relative latecomer, Agouron's Viracept has been able to compete with others that beat it to market by offering a drug many patients find easier to use.

Unlike Crixivan, which must be taken on an empty stomach with large quantities of water, Viracept can be taken at mealtime. While other protease drugs have been associated with severe nausea and the formation of kidney stones, Viracept's worst side effect appears to be diarrhea.

"The majority of the people taking Viracept are falling into the first-time protease user category," Johnson said. "But we are also seeing a fairly significant rate of patients switching (from other drugs)."
"You have an expanding market scenario," said Mehta and Isaly analyst Edmund Debler. "I think Merck has lost some market share but not enough to account for all of Viracept's sales."
Debler estimates the total market for protease inhibitors will reach $1 billion this year from $440 last year, saying there is room for growth for all the players.
Based on those prospects, he said he has a 12-month price target on Agouron stock of $120 a share, and said it is "possible" the shares could reach $160 in 24 months.
The stock dipped 3/8 on Friday to close at 95-3/8.
